opus-5.5.text:
I think the commercial value of agents comes from a very simple shift: we're moving from AI that answers to AI that does. For the past few years, most products were essentially chatbots. You ask a question, you get text back, and then a human still has to take that text and go do the actual work. The value is real, but it's capped, because the human is still the bottleneck.

An agent changes that. It can take a goal, break it into steps, call tools, browse, write and run code, check its own results, and keep going until the task is finished. Once a model can reliably complete a multi-step task end to end, you're no longer selling "a smarter search box." You're selling labor, or at least a slice of labor. And the market for labor is enormously bigger than the market for software.

The second reason is that a lot of the world's work is actually long-horizon but fairly structured. Think about data analysis, customer operations, filling forms across different systems, research and report writing, debugging code. These aren't tasks that need genius in any single step. They need persistence, the ability to recover from mistakes, and the ability to stitch many small actions together. That's exactly where reinforcement learning on top of strong base models has started to make a real difference. Models are learning not just to produce a plausible answer but to actually reach a verifiable outcome.

And third, agents create a much clearer way to measure value. With a chatbot, it's hard to say how much a good answer is worth. With an agent, you can say: this task used to take a person three hours, now it's done in twenty minutes with a review step. That's something a business can price and pay for.

Of course, we're still early. Reliability is the core issue. An agent that succeeds 70% of the time on a long task can be more frustrating than no agent at all, because you have to check everything. So I'd say the commercial value is real and very large, but it unlocks in steps: each time reliability on a certain class of tasks crosses a threshold, a whole category of work suddenly becomes automatable. That's why I'm optimistic, and also why I think the core competition is really about training: who can make agents robust enough on real tasks, not just impressive in demos.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can finish work that previously required a person, giving the example of a task reduced from three hours to twenty minutes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yi Wu: I think the simplest way to put it is that an agent is the first form of AI that actually does the work instead of advising you about the work. For a long time, what we sold was a model's output. You ask a question, you get an answer, and then a human still has to take that answer and carry it through all the remaining steps. That is useful, but the economic value is capped, because the human is still the bottleneck. They still have to open the tools, make the calls, check the results, fix the mistakes.

An agent changes where the value sits. Now the system can take a goal, break it down, operate in the environment, observe what happens, and keep going until the goal is met. Once you can do that, you are no longer selling intelligence as a consultation. You are selling completed outcomes. And companies have always paid for outcomes much more readily than they pay for insight. Nobody budgets for "good suggestions." They budget for tickets closed, code shipped, invoices reconciled, customers retained.

There is also a structural reason I believe in it. Most knowledge work is long-tailed and messy. It is not one hard reasoning problem, it is thirty small steps across five different systems with a lot of glue in between. That glue is exactly the work nobody wants to do and nobody can easily automate with traditional software, because the rules change every week. An agent that can read the situation and adapt is the first technology that fits that shape of problem.

The last point is that agents compound. A model answers one question and the interaction is over. An agent can run for hours, remember what it learned, and get better at a specific company's workflows. That means the value is not just per-query, it accrues. From a business perspective, that looks a lot more like hiring than like buying a tool, and the labor market is a very large market.

So I do not think the commercial value of agents is speculative. I think the hard part is reliability. Once an agent is trustworthy enough that you stop checking every step, the economics become very obvious.

r001.rationale: The response says agents carry tasks through remaining steps that humans would otherwise perform, reducing the human bottleneck and the need to handle or check each step.

astra-6.text:
I think the commercial value comes from moving AI from answering questions to actually completing work. An answer can be useful, but someone still has to take that answer, make decisions, and carry out the next steps. An agent can potentially handle more of that process.

Take customer support. The goal isn’t simply to produce a good reply. It’s to understand the issue, check the relevant records, take an authorized action, and verify that the problem is resolved. If an agent can reliably do that, the business can measure its value in time saved and issues resolved.

But reliability is the key. A compelling demo doesn’t automatically make a valuable product. If people have to check every step or constantly fix mistakes, the benefit shrinks. So I think the strongest commercial opportunities are in well-defined workflows where agents have the right tools, clear limits, and a way to ask for human help. That’s where their capabilities can translate into real economic value.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can complete more of the work and that businesses can measure their value in time saved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the commercial value comes from turning intelligence into completed work. A model can give you an answer, but an agent can take a goal, carry out several steps, and use feedback to adjust what it does. That brings it closer to something a customer can actually pay for.

For example, if you want to resolve a customer’s issue, generating a good reply is only one part of the job. You may also need to look up an order, check a policy, and take an action. If an agent can handle that process reliably, it can save time and improve the service.

The key word is reliably. Being able to demonstrate a task once doesn’t establish commercial value. You need to complete it consistently, at a reasonable cost, and know when to ask a person for help. I think that’s where the real opportunity is.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent that handles the task process can save time, attributing commercial value to reduced time spent completing tasks.
